candidates.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Didymos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its trajectory. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA The European Space Agency’s BepiColombo mission has successfully entered orbit around Mercury despite a software glitch that resulted in a shorter-than-planned thruster burn. According to the agency’s 23 November update, the BepiColombo spacecraft reoriented itself at 17:51 CET on 21 November, resulting in a planned loss of communications with Earth. At 19:24 CET, the spacecraft fired its four chemical thrusters as it passed approximately 635 kilometres above Mercury’s surface. The burn was scheduled to last 37 minutes, with communications expected to resume at 22:37 CET. However, the agency did not publicly confirm that contact had been re-established until 03:02 CET on 22 November. In its initial update, the agency confirmed that the spacecraft had achieved orbital capture around Mercury and that ground teams were assessing telemetry. According to ESA’s subsequent account of the manoeuvre, orbital capture had been confirmed internally at approximately 01:00 CET. It was not until 20:15 CET on 22 November that the agency revealed that the thruster burn had been shorter than planned due to a software issue. In a more detailed breakdown published on 23 November, ESA explained that when it re-established contact with the spacecraft, teams discovered that it had entered safe mode. “Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened,” said ESA’s BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco. Teams at ESA and spacecraft manufacturer Airbus have traced the anomaly to a software issue affecting the spacecraft’s orientation and thruster control, although investigations are ongoing. According to ESA, the burn achieved just 77% of its intended change in velocity. While this did not prevent the spacecraft from achieving orbital capture, it entered a 75-hour orbit around Mercury instead of the planned 58-hour orbit. candidates.title: China, Pakistan to conduct cooperative space station experiments
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China and Pakistan will conduct four cooperative scientific experiments aboard China Space Station, involving cyanobacteria, quinoa seeds and two types of composite materials, according to  the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The Pakistani astronaut on a short-term flight on China Space Station will carry out related experimental operations in orbit.

One of the experiments, proposed by Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission, will examine how cyanobacteria grow and absorb carbon dioxide in space, providing data for future oxygen regeneration and biological production. Cyanobacteria are tiny organisms that use sunlight to grow and release oxygen. The organisms used in the experiment come from Pakistan.

Another experiment, led by the University of Agriculture Faisalabad, will expose 32 quinoa seed samples to the space environment to study their resilience and longevity.

Two materials experiments will test the protective performance of graphene-based composites and the repair efficiency of self-healing carbon fiber composites.

The Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will take a short-term flight on China Space Station, will carry out related experimental operations in orbit, according to Chen Mengyun, International Cooperation Project Manager at the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Chinese and Pakistani scientific teams will also jointly publish papers and share the results of the experiments, said Chen.

The space station will continue to solicit, select and implement new space science projects, Chen said.

She added that China Space Station, also the national space laboratory, is open to scientists worldwide. It solicits proposals for space science and application projects from global scientists on an ongoing basis each year.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms. But in the end, Blue Origin did it first. Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket. Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects. But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown. candidates.title: UK joins 10 other nations in NATO STARLIFT satellite launch initiative
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The UK has joined 10 other countries in a NATO-led initiative to develop a network of flexible satellite launch services, aiming to ensure more reliable access to space and strengthen security.

The UK Ministry of Defence announced on Sunday that the country had signed the NATO STARLIFT initiative alongside Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Türkiye and the Republic of Korea.

STARLIFT aims to work with commercial launch providers and spaceport operators to build a network of launch capabilities across participating countries, making access to space more resilient, responsive and cost-effective.

According to NATO, the initiative will help military users secure launch slots on commercial rockets, including for urgent satellite launches. It will also support improvements to launch infrastructure, logistics and air and maritime traffic management to ensure safe launch operations.

NATO announced the initiative on November 17, following a funding commitment by the participating countries through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency. The agreement was signed in Brussels on October 29.

The UK government said joining STARLIFT supports its updated Space Strategy, published this year, which calls for stronger collective defense through NATO by sharing capabilities, ensuring reliable access to space and improving interoperability among allies. The strategy outlines more than 7.8 billion pounds (about $10.2 billion) in investment to secure the UK's interests and drive growth in the space sector.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered From its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station. The Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs). As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together. candidates.title: 10 things that worry me about chasing the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt. A dust storm could make the eclipsed sun less impressive. (Image credit: Grant Faint via Getty Images) 1. A sudden dust storm The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view.
